content: Data and other sources of information, such as surveys, are critical for determining whether HIV programs are achieving their goals and addressing the needs of individuals affected by HIV. This information, when combined, can guide policy and programmatic decisions to address identified gaps effectively. Mechanisms should be established to ensure that findings from community-led monitoring (CLM) are shared with health facility managers and community-led organizations. A collaborative approach is recommended, involving stakeholders such as ministries and funding partners, to triangulate data from various sources, interpret it, and use it for evidence-based actions. In some settings, data observatories have been created, comprising community-led organizations and other stakeholders. These observatories have proven to be effective in sharing and analyzing data and formulating recommendations to improve program planning, policy, and service delivery. Additionally, in certain contexts, community-led organizations conducting CLM are included in Country Coordinating Mechanisms, National HIV/AIDS Councils, and other decision-making bodies to strengthen the integration of CLM with other strategic information processes. To ensure the systematic inclusion and sustainability of CLM, community groups require technical, financial, and material resources to support systems that collect data in formats compatible with national systems. However, in many settings, investment in community-led networks and organizations is insufficient, limiting their capacity to lead and deliver CLM. Reference groups, including experts from academic institutions, representatives from national HIV programs, government officials, and other stakeholders, can be formed to support community groups in undertaking CLM. Ultimately, policymakers, healthcare providers, data analysts, and community members all have a vested interest in improving access, experiences, and health outcomes for clients through enhanced service delivery. Advocacy driven by community-led organizations, integrating routine person-centered data with CLM findings in an inclusive multi-stakeholder process, can provide insights into unmet needs and gaps that might otherwise be overlooked. An uninterrupted supply of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs and diagnostic commodities for HIV prevention, testing, and treatment is essential for all HIV programs. A sustainable and efficient supply chain system for these drugs and commodities is complex and involves multiple stakeholders. A well-managed distribution system ensures that drugs remain in good condition, optimizes storage and transportation, minimizes theft and fraud, and provides accurate information for forecasting needs. The supply of ARVs must be continuous and uninterrupted at all service delivery points, as treatment interruptions can lead to the development and transmission of drug-resistant HIV, with potentially severe public health consequences. With the implementation of differentiated service delivery (DSD), drug data can serve as a valuable measure of multi-month dispensing, allowing for granular assessments of clinic visit frequencies at district and facility levels. Data on the months’ supply of drugs dispensed can reveal patterns across a country and contribute to evaluating the efficiency and outcomes of differentiated care. Linking drug supply data with aggregated, de-duplicated individual-level data can improve accuracy in estimating stock levels, enhance forecasting and procurement, and reduce drug wastage. Inaccuracies in patient data, such as loss to follow-up or duplicate entries, can result in significant drug wastage or stock-outs, as well as inappropriate budgeting and inefficient use of resources. Interoperable systems that link logistics management information systems (LMIS) with de-duplicated, aggregated, and anonymized or de-identified individual-level data can improve stock level estimation, forecasting, and procurement, ultimately reducing drug wastage. In Malawi, the Ministry of Health’s Department of HIV/AIDS and Viral Hepatitis developed a comprehensive HIV program management information system (DHAMIS) that includes a supply chain module for tracking and allocating ARVs and other HIV program commodities. DHAMIS integrates HIV program and logistics data from all facilities and central warehouse stock data into a single system. This implementation has resulted in highly accurate mid-term forecasts for all major regimens and minimal losses and stock-outs through proactive redistribution of supplies and visibility of site-level expiries and wastages. The Malawi Ministry of Health has achieved this success using paper records and quarterly site visits. Civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems provide essential data on births, deaths, and causes of death, which are critical for measuring HIV-related mortality. The completeness and accuracy of vital registration data vary significantly among countries. The utility of CRVS data for monitoring the health sector’s response to HIV depends on strict compliance with reporting requirements, including both primary and underlying causes of death, confidentiality for stigmatized causes of death such as HIV, and consistent, complete, and accurate civil registration across populations and geographic areas. Additional data from verbal autopsies, mortuary surveillance, and minimally invasive autopsies can help estimate HIV-related mortality and adjust for biases in weak CRVS systems. Linking routine HIV data with other systems that measure deaths and causes of death can enhance the completeness and value of information for both systems. Population-based surveys are crucial for capturing the situation of individuals not engaged in health services. For example, understanding why 30% of individuals are not receiving ART treatment in a country with 70% coverage requires a population-based survey that reaches a representative group of people not engaged with health services. These surveys complement routine program data and are often used to measure disease prevalence, risk behaviors, stigma, discrimination, and health service use and coverage. Biomarkers collected through these surveys can estimate HIV prevalence, incidence, viral load suppression, and other health outcomes. Key considerations when using population-based survey data include their resource-intensive nature, periodic implementation, and ability to provide precise estimates only at larger geographic levels. Managers and stakeholders may rely on more frequent and granular routine health information system (HIS) data while using survey data to periodically calibrate and assess the representativeness of routine findings. Probability surveys of key populations use specialized sampling methods to obtain representative samples of marginalized, mobile individuals with varying risk levels. However, generalizing or aggregating these results for national-level estimates should be done cautiously, considering potential limitations. Consistent methodologies, sampling strategies, and locations in recurring key population surveillance can improve comparability and trend monitoring. Mathematical modeling is essential for estimating the number of people newly infected with HIV or who have died from AIDS-related causes. This modeling provides critical insights into the potential impact of interventions and the overall trajectory of the epidemic.
